newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends mixed in US after setting fresh highs.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends mixed in US after setting fresh highs.

text.p: The dollar surged to its highest level in almost four years against the Japanese yen on Tuesday, buoyed by further evidence that the G3 nations are willing to tolerate current dollar strength.
But the dollar ended the day mostly lower against European currencies after initially rising to its highest level in over two and a half years against the German mark and the Swiss franc.
Dealers said the dollar's gains against the yen originated overseas after a Japanese finance official said the yen's recent slide was not a cause for immediate concern.
Gains were reinforced when Juergen Stark of the German finance ministry referred to dollar gains against the mark as a "normalization" of imbalances between the two currencies.

These comments were a signal to many in the market that, despite its sharp recent rise, support for a strong dollar remains firm. In the absence of any dollar-negative statements on Tuesday, dealers said the dollar's upward momentum against the yen continued.
"Nobody talked the dollar down so it had only one way to move," said Ben Strauss, assistant vice president at Bank Julius Baer and Co.
The dollar ended the day at 120.95/05 yen, up from 120.64/69 at the open. It reached a peak of 121.77 yen during the trading session, its highest level since February of 1993.
Against the mark, the dollar retreated from sharp early gains to close at 1.6477/82 against 1.6508/13 at the open. Early Tuesday it reached a high of 1.6570 marks, its best level since June of 1994.
A benign report on U.S. labor costs, which soothed fears of inflation and fueled early gains in the stock and bond markets pushed the dollar to its highs of the day.

The Labor Department reported on Tuesday that its Employment Cost Index, a measure of wage and benefits costs, rose by 0.8 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996, less than Wall Street economists had anticipated.
The bond market welcomed the news as a sign that wage-driven inflation was under control, jumping sharply after the release of the numbers, and creating a ripple effect in U.S. stocks and the dollar.
But late profit-taking in the stock and bond markets pushed the dollar off its highs late in the day.
"The dollar was really tied to the bonds and stocks," said John Hazelton, chief dealer at Manufacturers and Traders Bank.

The Dow Jones industrials ended the day down around 4 points at 6656 after rising as much as 100 points early in the session. The bellwether 30-year Treasury bond was only modestly higher in late trade after rising well over a point early.

In contrast to Friday of last week, when talk of Bank of Japan intervention took the dollar sharply off its highs against the Japanese currency, Tuesday's action was relatively quiet on the rumor front.
Talk did surface that the Federal Reserve was monitoring exchange rate fluctuations on behalf of the Bank of Japan, but the rumors did little to stem the dollar's upward momentum against the yen.

"I think they're concerned about the pace but not necessarily the level," said Doug Lee, corporate foreign exchange dealer at Sakura Bank Ltd, referring to the Group of Seven industrial nations. "They want to make sure the pace is stabilized and that it doesn't go up too fast too soon which it has recently."
In other trade on Tuesday, the dollar ended slightly weaker at 1.4270/80 Swiss francs against 1.4290/00 at the open. The British pound rose to $1.6170/80 against $1.6080/90 at the open.
The dollar fell modestly to Canadian $1.3397/02 from C$1.3440/45, while the Australian dollar closed at $0.7688/93, down from $0.7712/17 at the open.
